    BAR H BAR RANCH AND NATURE PRESERVE’S FILING IN SUPPORT OF SAVE
               THE LAMPASAS’ APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13


        Scimitar Partners LP and Bar H Bar Land & Cattle Co. (collectively, “Bar H Bar Ranch

and Nature Preserve”) files this pleading in support of Save the Lampasas’ Appeal of SOAH Order

No. 13. Bar H Bar Ranch and Nature Preserve does not wish to retread the well-reasoned

arguments outlined in that appeal, but does want to reiterate that SOAH Order No. 13 erroneously

treats almost every disputed fact between the parties who requested a route adequacy hearing and

Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation

(“LCRA”) (collectively, “Joint Applicants”) in a light most favorable to the Joint Applicants while

foreclosing the property owners’ rights to present controverting evidence in a hearing. This is

despite the Joint Applicants having the burden of proof to establish that the routes presented in the

application are adequate. 1 Or the fact that the Commission has made clear that “it is not


1
 Application of Wood County Electric Cooperative, Inc. for a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity for a
Proposed Transmission Line in Wood County, Texas, Docket No. 32070, Order on Appeal of Order No. 8 at 6 (Oct.
31, 2006).

                                                      1
 Commission Staff or any intervenor’s obligation to prove that an application is not adequate.” 2 To

this end, SOAH Order No. 13 cites to a previous SOAH Order 3 as legal support stating that “[o]nce

applicant makes a prima facie showing that its application is adequate, the parties challenging route

adequacy "must present evidence showing the inadequacy of an application or routes and

presenting other superior routes.” 4 This is inconsistent with Commission precedent which as noted

earlier, holds the exact opposite of that previous SOAH order cited to in SOAH Order No. 13.

           To say that once the Joint Applicants make a prima facie showing the routes proposed in

the application are adequate, that the burden then shifts to the challenging parties ignores the

Commission’s clear directive in Docket No. 32070. The Commission was clear that neither

Commission Staff nor any intervenor has the obligation to prove that an application is not adequate,

the burden is with the Joint Applicants to prove it is adequate. This burden-shifting also creates a

higher bar for the intervenors challenging route adequacy than it does for the utilities who are

ultimately asking the Commission to grant them a taking right against landowners in this

proceeding. We would urge the Commission to accept the Appeal’s reasoning and hold the utilities

to a higher standard than just making a prima facie showing of route adequacy, when the stakes

for intervening parties are the loss of property that will be given to the utility to build a transmission

line.

           Further, without a route adequacy hearing to fully explore the facts in dispute, choosing

Joint Applicants’ version of facts at the expense of the parties challenging route adequacy is an

unreasonable decision that should be reversed. The purpose of a route adequacy hearing is to



2
    Id.
3
    Order No. 13 at 6-7 (May 15, 2026) (internal citation omitted).
4
    Id.

                                                            2
 explore those disputed facts as to whether the Joint Applicants provided a sufficient number of

routes for the Commission to choose from. Those whom Order No. 13 posits bearing the burden

of presenting evidence showing the inadequacy of routes can only do that in an evidentiary hearing,

which SOAH Order No. 13 refuses to convene. The Order adopts the wrong legal standard, then

refuses to grant the moving parties the means of meeting that incorrect standard. Even if the

Commission accepts SOAH Order No. 13’s position regarding burden shifting to the challenging

parties, the challenging parties must be allowed a meaningful ability to challenge that prima facie

showing of route adequacy via the one mechanism they are allowed, a route adequacy hearing. To

deny that, despite clearly disputed facts not only allows the Joint Applicants to lessen their own

burden in proving route adequacy inconsistent with Commission precedent, but it also denies the

intervening parties any meaningful challenge on top of that. We urge the Commission to reverse

SOAH Order No. 13 and give the intervenors the ability to, at the very least, present their case in

favor of challenging route adequacy.

           Lastly, it is clear that many in the Texas Legislature are concerned with this proceeding

which directly ties into concerns of route adequacy. At least twenty-five (25) state legislators

representing directly affected citizens filed a letter expressing profound concerns about this

proceeding and the implementation of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. 5 They further state “[a]s

the Texas Legislature prepares to review issues related to energy generation, storage, and

transmission ahead of the 90th Legislative Session, it is prudent to pause further progress on this

project. Taking time for a fuller policy review and broader public discussion will help ensure that

any long-term decisions are informed by a complete understanding of their potential impacts.” 6



5
    Legislative Correspondence (May 14, 2026).
6
    Id.

                                                   3
 This is further evidence that the Commission should not ignore important concerns when it comes

to route adequacy and that even those who passed the laws in question are highly concerned with

this proceeding. We think at the very least, these concerns require a meaningful ability to challenge

route adequacy via a hearing on route adequacy in this proceeding.

       For those reasons, we respectfully support Save the Lampasas’ appeal of SOAH Order No.

13 and request that the Commission reverse said order and require a route adequacy hearing to be

scheduled to allow a meaningful challenge of the number of routes offered by the Joint Applicants.

Based on the procedural schedule which would have this case go to hearing on only the routes

submitted in the application on June 8th, we support Commission consideration of this appeal at

the May 29, 2026 Open Meeting.




                                                 4
 Dated: May 20, 2026


                         Respectfully submitted,
